text: So, supposing you are an air traffic controller and you are controlling access to a single
runway where flights have to land and take off.
So, the air traffic control tower receives requests from the aircraft about their expected
arrival and departure times and these requests come at random time.
So, it's not that they come in the order of the time of the actual event.
So, we might first get a request for a landing in Chennai at 1623 and later on we might get
a request for a takeoff at 1612 which is actually earlier and then we might get another
arrival information at 1655 and then another earlier arrival information at 1618 and the
strategy that the control tower is supposed to follow is to give priority to the flight
with the earliest usage time.
So, this is a priority queue.
Each request goes into the queue but it has a priority depending on the expected time
that it is going to take place.
So, we could give a min heap representation and if we take these six requests in the order
that they come and we insert them into the min heap, then we will get the min heap that
we see on the right hand side.
And so, in this because 1612 happens to be the earliest event among these six, it will
automatically float up to the root and so it will be available to us as the next event
to process and then maybe two minutes before that event happens, we can send a signal
to the flight giving it clearance to takeoff.
So, suppose we have an extra requirement on this.
Not only do we want to give priority to the earliest event to happen, but we also want
to impose some minimum separation of planes to avoid any possibility of collisions on the
runway.
So, we say that two planes accessing the runway must be a minimum of three minutes apart.
Now, in this example, we can see that the rule is violated by the two events at 1653
So, what happens is that we should when we insert or we accept the request for 1655,
assuming it came after 1653, at this point, we should check that it is, whether it is
at least three minutes apart from all the current pending requests.
If not, we should send a message to the pilot saying 1655 is not possible.
You must move your takeoff or landing to 1656 or later.
Now, unfortunately, in the heap data structure, there is no easy way to do this.
So, when 1655 is added to the heap, we have to scan it against all the elements in the
heap in order to find out whether it is within three minutes of any of them.
So, this would be a linear scan.
So, all other operations in certain delete on the heap were logarithmic, but this, if
we want to impose this constraint that no two elements in the heap are within three minutes
of each other, then we would add an extra linear time cost to every insert and this would
then make a heap unviable for this kind of data.
So, one way to compute this kind of requirement is to be able to check the predecessor and
the successor.
In other words, given the list of values that we have, for any value, can we quickly compute
what is the previous in terms of the nearest smaller value and the next successor, what
is the nearest bigger value?
So, if you look at 1618 for example, then the next smaller value is here.
So, this is the predecessor, 1612 and the next bigger value is here.
So, this is the successor.
Now, this happens to be, it looks like there is some nice relationship within the heap
in terms of the tree structure between predecessor and successor, but if you look at a different
value for example, 1653, then we will find that the predecessor lies in a different branch
of the tree and the successor lies in the same branch.
So, there is no direct relationship between the tree structure of the heap and the predecessor
and the successor relation that we need.

So, in a binary search tree, the binary tree could have an arbitrary structure, but the
values are arranged in a specific way.
So, for each node with a value v, all the nodes below v smaller than v are in the left
subtree and all the values are bigger than v are the right subtree.
And we typically we will assume that there are no duplicate values.
So, for example, here if we look at a root node 5, then the left subtree of 5 contains
values 1, 2, 4 which are all the nodes in this tree smaller than 5 and the right subtree

Now, this is a property that is recursively satisfied throughout the tree.
So, if you look at the node 2 for example, its left child, left subtree is just the single

Likewise, if we look at 8 and there is only one value other than 8 in the subtree starting

So, we can have these kind of gaps unlike in heaps, we can have a gap but we have this
uniform property that at any node in the subtree all the values smaller than the node
